JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning

Xudong Wu Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong    Guangchen Lan Affiliation: Salesforce AI Research    Mingqi Yuan Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong    Jiayu Chen Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Correspondence to: jiayuc@hku.hk
Abstract

The performance of language agents depends jointly on model weights and the harness. Optimizing either alone can be constrained by the other component, limiting overall performance gains. Our analysis of naive alternating training reveals progressive incompatibility between the model and harness, which increasingly interferes with task execution and may also undermine model training, leading to performance degradation. To coordinate the evolution of models and harnesses, we introduce JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly train an executable harness generation policy and a task execution policy through reinforcement learning. JoMoHa outperforms the evaluated weight-only and harness-only baselines and achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld. By learning both task execution and runtime improvement from its own generated trajectories, JoMoHa performs recursive self-improvement (RSI).

Keywords: 
multi-agent reinforcement learning, language agents, joint harness–weight optimization

1 Introduction

A language agent consists of a model and a harness. The model weights determine its learned reasoning and decision-making capabilities, while the harness organizes how these capabilities are used. Improving an agent therefore admits two complementary paths: training its model weights and improving its harness.

Existing methods have made progress along both paths. Reinforcement learning methods train model weights from task feedback, improving the policy that makes decisions (Yu et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024). Alternatively, harness optimization changes the runtime surrounding the model (Lee et al., 2026; Shao et al., 2026). However, agent performance depends jointly on both components, and optimizing either alone can leave overall gains constrained by the other. The comparison with weight-only and harness-only training in Figure 1 further motivates learning model weights and harnesses together.

However, naively alternating updates to model weights and the harness does not ensure their compatibility. As the model changes, an existing harness may provide outdated or incorrect guidance that interferes with task execution and limits performance gains. Such guidance also shapes the experience used for training and may steer subsequent model updates toward less effective behavior, potentially worsening performance over time. We diagnose these issues through controlled comparisons and failure trajectory analysis in Section 4.

WHALE mitigates this issue through small alternating updates to model weights and harnesses. Its published instantiation updates model weights through online rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RSFT) rather than RL, and uses Meta-Harness search driven by a fixed external proprietary frontier model (Kim et al., 2026). However, harness optimization continues to rely on a fixed external proprietary frontier model to propose improvements. Execution feedback guides harness selection, but does not update the proposer itself. The capability to improve the harness therefore remains delegated to an external model rather than trained within the system. This motivates a different approach: making harness generation a trainable policy and using the same task execution outcome to train both the harness generator and the task performer.

We instantiate recursive self-improvement (RSI) by learning both task execution and harness construction from the system’s own generated programs, trajectories, and execution feedback. Harness-R1 supports the potential of this direction: its trained harness Engineer outperforms the evaluated fixed frontier editors, including proprietary models (Shao et al., 2026). However, it keeps the task-performing model frozen during Engineer training. This leaves an open question:

How can both policies improve through reinforcement learning from their shared task executions?

A natural starting point is to alternate updates to the two policies using task outcomes. Yet alternation alone does not ensure that their improvements remain compatible. We investigate this problem through controlled diagnosis of a long-phase alternating run in which performance initially improves and subsequently deteriorates (Section 4.1). By evaluating saved model checkpoints with and without the same fixed harness, we distinguish two sources of decline: the task-performing model loses ability, and the unchanged harness becomes more harmful as the model changes. In one task, a later model succeeds in 14 turns without a harness but reaches the 50-turn limit under the old harness (Table 3b). These findings motivate coordinating the two learners throughout training, rather than relying on alternation alone.

We introduce JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly train a harness-generation policy and a task-execution policy through reinforcement learning. We call the two policies the Engineer and the Solver. The Engineer generates an executable harness, and the Solver interacts with the environment under that harness. The generated program and its multi-turn execution form a paired training example (Figure 3). The shared task outcome trains both policies, each on its own generated tokens. Therefore, JoMoHa implements RSI: the improvement policy itself learns from execution feedback, alongside the task-performing policy. We release our code at https://github.com/xudongwu-0/coevolve.

We evaluate JoMoHa on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, where it achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods: 97.0%, 45.8%, and 68.0%, respectively (Section 6.1, Table 4).

To coordinate the Engineer and Solver, JoMoHa combines collaboration-aware value estimation, role-specific return normalization, partner-trajectory weighting, and asymmetric update schedules. We examine these design choices through component studies in Section 6.2.

Our contributions are threefold:

  1. 1.

    Diagnosing failure in alternating training. Fixed-component tests distinguish declining Solver capability from worsening harness compatibility. Trajectory analysis reveals how incorrect harness state disrupts otherwise successful execution. Together, these findings highlight risks to both task execution and continued learning, motivating compatibility-aware joint training.

  2. 2.

    Joint model–harness reinforcement learning. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first framework to jointly train an executable-harness generation policy and a task-execution policy through RL. The Engineer and Solver learn from the same task outcome, making both harness construction and task execution trainable within a shared learning process.

  3. 3.

    Coordination adaptations and empirical evaluation. We adapt cooperative-learning mechanisms to the Engineer–Solver setting and evaluate JoMoHa across three environments. Frozen-Engineer controls, fixed-Solver harness comparisons, and component studies assess the benefits of training the Engineer, improving the harness, and coordinating the two policies.

2 Related Work

Model-weight optimization.

Reinforcement learning improves language-model reasoning and decision-making from task feedback (Shao et al., 2024). Single-Rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) uses one rollout per prompt, a learned value model, and token-level calibration to stabilize asynchronous agentic RL (Hou et al., 2026). For tool-using agents, Search-R1 learns when and how to retrieve information (Jin et al., 2025), while ReTool learns to interleave reasoning with code execution (Feng et al., 2025). RAGEN studies the training dynamics of multi-turn agents (Wang et al., 2025). These methods improve the task-performing policy under a prescribed runtime, rather than jointly learning a separate policy that constructs that runtime. JoMoHa trains the Solver alongside an Engineer whose generated harness shapes the Solver’s execution.

Harness optimization.

A complementary line improves the system surrounding the model. ReAct organizes reasoning and action, while Self-Refine and Reflexion use textual feedback to revise behavior (Yao et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). OPRO and DSPy support instruction and pipeline optimization (Yang et al., 2023; Khattab et al., 2023). ADAS and AFlow search over agent architectures and executable workflows (Hu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), and Meta-Harness searches executable harnesses using prior code, scores, and execution traces (Lee et al., 2026). These approaches motivate treating the runtime as an optimization object, but improving a program does not necessarily train its generator. Harness-R1 makes runtime editing a learned capability by training an Engineer through RL against a frozen target agent (Shao et al., 2026). JoMoHa further trains the Solver alongside the Engineer, allowing both policies to adapt to their changing partner.

Joint learning and coordination.

WHALE jointly improves model weights and harnesses through alternating updates (Kim et al., 2026). Its published instantiation combines online RSFT with Meta-Harness search driven by a fixed external proprietary frontier model. Compared with WHALE, JoMoHa learns the harness-generating policy itself and trains both policies through RL from the same executed program–rollout pair (Table 1).

Cooperative RL provides foundations for learning from team outcomes (Yu et al., 2022; Foerster et al., 2017a; Kuba et al., 2021; Foerster et al., 2017b; van Hasselt et al., 2016). These classical methods were primarily developed and evaluated in non-language environments. Adapting these ideas to LLM training, particularly our program-mediated setting, is nontrivial: the Engineer and Solver have separate token histories and different decision horizons, while the Engineer’s program shapes the Solver’s entire multi-turn rollout. Their execution conditions also change as both policies learn. Our adaptations address critic information, role-specific return scales, partner-trajectory weighting, and update frequency. Component studies examine their contributions in this setting, and the complete coordination design improves performance over the Joint-only baseline (Section 6.2).

3 Background

Reinforcement learning (RL) improves a policy, a distribution over actions, through interaction and reward (Sutton and Barto, 2018). A Markov decision process (MDP) describes this interaction using states, actions, transition dynamics, and rewards: the next state depends on the current state and action. An episode is one task attempt. Language agents observe only part of the environment, so their policies use the available history. An actor is the trainable policy; a critic predicts its future return and provides a baseline for advantages—whether an outcome is better or worse than expected.

For a task xx, the Engineer uses evidence ee to sample a proposal trajectory τE\tau_{\mathrm{E}}. Validation and fallback map it to the executed harness h=𝒱⁡(τE)h=\mathcal{V}(\tau_{\mathrm{E}}). The Solver acts under hh, producing trajectory τS\tau_{\mathrm{S}} and terminal task reward R⁡(x,τS)R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}}). For role i∈{E,S}i\in\{\mathrm{E},\mathrm{S}\}, θi\theta_{i} and ϕi\phi_{i} are actor and critic parameters, with actor policy πθi\pi_{\theta_{i}}. Indices tt, bb, and kk denote generated-token positions, paired episodes, and saved checkpoints, respectively; θS(k)\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(k)} and hkh_{k} identify saved weights and code. The no-harness condition ∅\varnothing retains the base executor.

SAO learns from one rollout per prompt using a critic (Hou et al., 2026). Both roles share the task reward, while their returns also include role-specific KL penalties that restrain divergence from fixed reference policies.

4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together?

We examine an alternating-training baseline that updates the Solver and Engineer in separate phases. Such training may lead to over-adaptation between the Solver and its harness: each component adapts to a counterpart that subsequently changes, potentially making their learned behavior less compatible. On ALFWorld, this baseline initially improves from 83.0% to 90.5%, but then deteriorates across successive stages to 31.5% (Table 2). In comparison, JoMoHa reaches 97.0%. We analyze the alternating run to investigate how harness mismatch can affect both task execution and Solver learning.

4.1 Diagnosing Model–Harness Compatibility

The stage-level results alone cannot distinguish declining Solver ability from worsening harness compatibility, because both components change across stages. We therefore hold one harness fixed and evaluate it with different Solver checkpoints.

The percentage success SR⁡(θS,h)\mathrm{SR}(\theta_{\mathrm{S}},h) evaluates fixed Solver weights under a saved harness. The no-harness condition h=∅h=\varnothing removes the learned harness while retaining the base executor. The harness contribution to a fixed Solver is

Δh​(θS,h)=SR⁡(θS,h)−SR⁡(θS,∅).\Delta_{h}(\theta_{\mathrm{S}},h)=\mathrm{SR}(\theta_{\mathrm{S}},h)-\mathrm{SR}(\theta_{\mathrm{S}},\varnothing). (1)

This comparison separates Solver performance without the learned harness from the harness’s immediate effect on execution.

Specifically, we select earlier Solver weights θS(2)\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(2)}, later weights θS(3)\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(3)}, and the saved harness h2h_{2} from the alternating run. For each Solver, we evaluate the same fixed harness and the no-harness condition on the same ALFWorld evaluation tasks. The following aggregate comparisons and trajectory analyses examine both execution interference and Solver degradation.

Separating execution interference from Solver degradation.

Table 3 reveals two distinct changes. Across each row, adding the same harness reduces success by 4.0 points for θS(2)\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(2)} but 17.0 points for θS(3)\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(3)}: its negative effect increases by 13.0 points. Down the no-harness column, success falls from 82.5% to 48.0%: the Solver loses 34.5 points even when the learned harness is removed. Together, these account for the decline under the fixed harness:

−47.5⏟system decline=−34.5⏟Solver decline+−13.0⏟compatibility loss.\underbrace{-47.5}_{\text{system decline}}=\underbrace{-34.5}_{\text{Solver decline}}+\underbrace{-13.0}_{\text{compatibility loss}}. (2)

The first comparison shows that an unchanged harness can increasingly interfere with execution as the Solver changes. The additional loss cannot be explained by the Engineer generating a worse new harness. At θS(3)\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(3)}, adding h2h_{2} changes success to failure on 18.0% of evaluation tasks and failure to success on 1.0%.

The second comparison shows that removing the harness does not restore the later Solver’s earlier performance. The decline therefore extends beyond interference during the current execution. It is consistent with the concern that training under mismatched harnesses may steer the Solver toward less effective behavior. These findings motivate maintaining Solver–harness compatibility throughout training, rather than treating the harness only as an inference-time aid.

Case 1: Harness-induced failure on ALFWorld.

We examine evaluation trajectories produced by the earlier and later Solver checkpoints from the alternating training run analyzed above. The task requires cleaning a sponge and placing it on a cart. The later Solver succeeds in 14 turns without the learned harness, but reaches the 50-turn limit under the old harness h2h_{2} (Table 3b). The earlier Solver succeeds in both conditions, taking 16 and 14 turns, respectively. The later Solver therefore retains the behavior needed to complete this task; the failure appears when it is combined with the old harness.

The trajectory analysis reveals the following failure sequence:

  1. 1.

    The environment advances. Cleaning has completed, so the remaining work is to finish navigation and placement.

  2. 2.

    The harness fails to update its state. The executed action is stored in a nested field, but the old lookup uses a literal dotted key. The correct access is on the first line below; the old lookup is on the second:

    ctx["action"]["final_action"]
ctx.get("action.final_action")

    A dotted string is a different dictionary key, not a nested lookup, so the completed action is missed. A second state update can also overwrite earlier inventory evidence when the current observation omits the word indicating cleaning.

  3. 3.

    Stale guidance sends execution backward. Although the environment has confirmed cleaning, the harness continues directing the Solver to find and clean the object. The episode loops through navigation and reaches the turn limit.

Case 2: Solver failure without the learned harness.

A contrasting ALFWorld case from the same training run exposes a failure in the no-harness condition. After cleaning a potato and navigating to the destination, the later Solver omits the final placement action and eventually reaches the turn limit. Because no learned harness is active, this failure cannot be attributed to interference from h2h_{2}. It illustrates why removing an incompatible harness alone cannot address all failures of the trained Solver.

4.2 From Compatibility to Coordinated Learning

Taken together, these findings suggest that a mismatched harness can impair current task execution and may also distort the experience from which the Solver learns. This creates a risk of a negative feedback loop in which ineffective harness guidance and declining Solver capability reinforce one another. Maintaining a compatible Solver–harness pair throughout learning is therefore important.

Our unit of learning is a complete task attempt: the generated harness, the actions taken under it, and the final outcome. The Engineer learns to generate effective harnesses, while the Solver learns to complete tasks under them. To mitigate this risk, our method uses their shared task outcome to coordinate value estimation and policy updates, supporting the joint adaptation of both policies.

5 JoMoHa

JoMoHa jointly trains two LLM policies: an Engineer that generates a harness and a Solver that performs tasks under it. Both learn from the outcome of the same task attempt (Figure 3). To coordinate their learning, we use collaboration-aware value estimation, role-specific return normalization, partner-trajectory weighting, and asymmetric update schedules.

5.1 Learning from a Shared Task Outcome

For a task xx, the Engineer receives historical feedback ee and samples a proposal trajectory τE\tau_{\mathrm{E}}. Validation and fallback map that proposal to the executed harness h=𝒱⁡(τE)h=\mathcal{V}(\tau_{\mathrm{E}}). The Solver then interacts with the environment under hh, producing trajectory τS\tau_{\mathrm{S}} and task reward R⁡(x,τS)R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}}). An invalid proposal maps to h=∅h=\varnothing, retaining the base executor.

The two policies share the objective

J⁡(θE,θS)=𝔼x,e,h,τS​[R⁡(x,τS)],J(\theta_{\mathrm{E}},\theta_{\mathrm{S}})=\mathbb{E}_{x,e,h,\tau_{\mathrm{S}}}\left[R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}})\right], (3)

where hh is the validation/fallback result and τS\tau_{\mathrm{S}} is collected by the Solver under that harness. The task reward is binary on ALFWorld.

The same reward trains both policies: the Engineer learns which harnesses support successful execution, while the Solver learns how to complete tasks under those harnesses. Each policy is updated on its own generated outputs, without differentiating through harness execution. We use a KL-regularized SAO-based actor–critic backbone (Hou et al., 2026), with a fixed reference policy for each role. The local realization retains behavior–proximal token-ratio decoupling.

5.2 Value Estimation for Two Different Roles

Each policy has an independent critic that estimates its expected return, including task rewards and its own KL penalty. The critics provide baselines for computing advantages: whether an outcome is better or worse than expected.

Context: account for collaboration conditions.

The usefulness of an Engineer proposal depends on the Solver, while the Solver’s performance depends on the harness. A critic Vϕi​(zi,t,ci)V_{\phi_{i}}(z_{i,t},c_{i}) predicts the role’s expected remaining regularized return from its current history zi,tz_{i,t} and a short collaboration summary cic_{i}. The supplemental fields describe the task identifier, training version, and role-specific execution conditions. The task field is a path or identifier, not a full environment observation. Context is provided only to the critics and does not change the actors’ inputs.

ValueNorm: account for different return scales.

The Engineer generates a harness once, whereas the Solver acts over multiple turns. Their different output lengths and KL penalties can produce different return scales despite the shared task reward. Writing the raw, unweighted critic target as Gi,tG_{i,t}, we normalize critic targets separately for each role:

G^i,t\displaystyle\widehat{G}_{i,t} =Gi,t−miσi,\displaystyle=\frac{G_{i,t}-m_{i}}{\sigma_{i}},
Vϕi​(zi,t,ci)\displaystyle V_{\phi_{i}}(z_{i,t},c_{i}) =σi​V^ϕi​(zi,t,ci)+mi,\displaystyle=\sigma_{i}\widehat{V}_{\phi_{i}}(z_{i,t},c_{i})+m_{i}, (4)

where mim_{i} and σi>0\sigma_{i}>0 are running return statistics. Values are restored to their original scale before advantages are computed. Hats denote normalized targets and predictions. This critic-target normalization is separate from standardizing actor advantages.

5.3 Coordinating Policy Updates

We compute advantages using generalized advantage estimation (Schulman et al., 2016) and standardize them separately for the two policies. We introduce two additional mechanisms to account for the changing partner and the different adaptation needs of the two roles.

Peer: weight experience using the partner’s trajectory.

As both policies change, a recorded task attempt may become more or less representative of their current collaboration. Peer adjusts its influence using the paired partner trajectory:

A~E,b,t=wS,b​A¯E,b,t,A~S,b,t=wE,b​A¯S,b,t,\widetilde{A}_{\mathrm{E},b,t}=w_{\mathrm{S},b}\bar{A}_{\mathrm{E},b,t},\qquad\widetilde{A}_{\mathrm{S},b,t}=w_{\mathrm{E},b}\bar{A}_{\mathrm{S},b,t}, (5)

where A¯i,b,t\bar{A}_{i,b,t} is the role-standardized advantage. Each partner weight compares the likelihood of the recorded trajectory under the policy snapshot used for the current update with its likelihood when collected. We bound the weight to [0.5,2][0.5,2], treat it as a constant during optimization, and leave critic targets unchanged.

Schedule: give the Solver additional adaptation.

Changing the Engineer changes the harnesses under which the Solver learns. To give the Solver additional adaptation without another Engineer update, the coordination study repeats joint, joint, Solver-only rounds. The resulting update ratio is Engineer:Solver =2:3=2:3.

Solver-only rounds freeze the Engineer’s parameters but still sample fresh harnesses. They use unit partner weights. Thus, the Solver continues learning under sampled harnesses while their generating policy remains fixed.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure. At deployment, we select a saved harness and evaluate it with a frozen Solver checkpoint.

6 Experiments

Experimental setup.

We evaluate JoMoHa on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, which test household task completion, goal-directed shopping, and database interaction, respectively (Shridhar et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024). We report success rates in all three environments, a separate WebShop score, and the equally weighted mean of the three success rates. The ALFWorld coordination study uses separate Qwen3.5-9B-class Engineer and Solver actors with independent critics, initialized from Agent SFT, and collects eight paired episodes per round for 144 rounds.

Baselines.

Except for locally evaluated JoMoHa and WHALE, scores are taken from Harness-R1 (Shao et al., 2026); we use its training and test sets, with checkpoint and harness selection on a separate validation set. The task model is Qwen3.5-9B; frontier model names denote harness editors, not replacement Solvers. Agent SFT + Harness-R1 additionally fine-tunes the task model, while WHALE uses its RSFT-plus-search recipe. WHALE alternates after eight environment interactions (16 training steps), uses the same harness-search settings as JoMoHa, and matches its total environment-interaction budget. Section 6.2 examines one-sided learning, frozen-Engineer training, program swaps, and coordination components.

6.1 Main Results

JoMoHa achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on all three benchmarks: 97.0% on ALFWorld, 45.8% on WebShop, and 68.0% on DBBench (Table 4). Its average success is 70.3%, exceeding Agent SFT + Harness-R1 by 6.1 percentage points and WHALE by 7.2 points. The gains over WHALE are 16.5, 2.4, and 2.7 points across the three environments, respectively.

The ALFWorld breakdown locates the largest gains on tasks that transform an object’s state before placement. Against the strongest competing result in each category, JoMoHa gains 18.2 points on Clean, 17.3 on Heat, and 24.8 on Cool, compared with 0.0–4.0 points on the remaining categories. This pattern extends beyond differences in ceiling effects: on Heat and Cool, the gains remove approximately 83.6% and 89.9% of the respective best competitor’s errors . These tasks require execution to distinguish a completed transformation from the remaining navigation and placement, making the results consistent with the state-tracking issue diagnosed in Section 4.1. Pick2 remains the weakest category at 91.8%, indicating remaining room for improvement when multiple objects must be collected and placed.

6.2 Ablation Studies

We examine three sources of improvement: training the Engineer rather than only resampling its outputs, improving the harness at fixed Solver weights, and coordinating the two policies beyond the Joint-only baseline.

Training the Engineer beyond fresh harness sampling.

Frozen Engineer fixes the initial Engineer parameters while continuing to sample fresh harnesses and train the Solver. It reaches 90.5% at step 144, versus 97.0% for JoMoHa (Figure 1); even its best reported checkpoint, 91.5% at step 108, remains 5.5 points below the complete method. Thus, the gap persists when the control can both resample programs and use its best reported checkpoint. Weight-only and Harness-only reach 89.5% and 80.5%, respectively. Together, these controls favor training both policies over the evaluated one-sided recipes, while the component study below examines the additional benefit of coordination.

Harness utility at unchanged Solver weights.

Learning curves alone cannot separate improvements in Solver ability from improvements in the generated runtime. We therefore cross-evaluate saved programs and Solver checkpoints (Table 5). At the later Solver, replacing the initial program with the later program raises success from 92.5% to 96.5%, without changing model weights. Relative to no harness, the later program gains 5.0 points, with no observed success-to-failure regressions on this evaluation set. The earlier and later learned programs also both improve the earlier Solver from 91.5% under the initial program to 95.0%. These results show that the saved programs contribute useful behavior beyond the initial runtime, including at a different Solver checkpoint. The equal 95.0% scores on the earlier Solver, but 95.0% versus 96.5% on the later Solver, further show that program value depends on the Solver with which it is paired.

Coordinating the two learners.

Joint-only trains both policies from paired task outcomes without Context, ValueNorm, Peer, or Schedule. Adding each mechanism separately raises its final success from 88.5% to 91.5–92.5%; combining all four reaches 97.0%, an 8.5-point improvement over Joint-only (Table 6). Context yields the highest single-addition point estimate, 92.5%, consistent with the value of informing each critic about its collaboration conditions. Schedule and Peer both achieve 92.0%, while ValueNorm achieves 91.5%.

7 Discussion and Conclusion

One model learns to write the runtime; another learns to act under it. JoMoHa trains both from the same task result while keeping their token histories and value estimates separate. Fixed-component tests measure the two sides of this interaction. At fixed Solver weights, saved programs improve on the initial code. Learning the writer outperforms freezing it while still sampling new code, and coordinating the two learners improves on joint updates alone. The complete system has the highest reported success on all three environments in the benchmark table, averaging 70.3%. This is RSI through execution feedback: both the task policy and the policy that constructs its runtime are learned within the system.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
